client: I've been feeling really on edge lately, and I guess that's why I'm here. My partner moved in with me about a month ago, and I didn't expect it to be this hard — the apartment is constantly messy and it's stressing me out way more than I thought it would. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the mess is still going to be there when I get home tonight.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — the stress of a big life change on top of feeling like nothing will actually shift, which can make it hard to even feel hopeful about being here. That sense of "what's the point?" is really worth paying attention to, because it often tells us something important about how overwhelmed we're feeling underneath. I'm curious — when you imagine walking into that messy apartment tonight, what's the feeling that comes up most strongly for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I picture walking in there tonight, the first thing I feel is just... dread. Like this heavy weight that settles in my chest before I even open the door. It's not just the mess, it's more like the mess is proof of something — proof that I can't get it together, that I'm failing at even the basic stuff of living alone.
therapist: That word "proof" really stands out to me — it sounds like the mess has become more than just clutter, it's turned into evidence your mind is using to build a case against yourself. That's such a painful place to be, where something external keeps feeding this inner narrative that you're failing. I'd love to gently challenge that thought together — what do you think it would mean about you if the apartment *were* perfectly tidy?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess if it were perfectly tidy it would mean... I don't know, that I have my life together? But that feels almost impossible to imagine right now, and honestly even thinking about it makes me anxious, like I'm setting myself up to fail again. It's like I can't even picture a clean apartment without immediately thinking about how long it would stay that way before I let it fall apart again.
therapist: There's something really telling in how quickly your mind jumps from imagining success straight to the moment it falls apart — like your brain won't even let you have the win for a second before it's already planning for the failure. That pattern, where you're essentially pre-punishing yourself before anything has even gone wrong, is something we can really work with in CBT. I'm wondering — whose voice does that sound like, the one that's so certain you'll let things fall apart?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I didn't expect it. I think... honestly, it sounds like my own voice, but maybe it started as my dad's — he had this way of pointing out everything that could go wrong before you even tried something, like he was protecting you but it just felt like he didn't believe in you. And now I've just... absorbed it so completely that I can't tell where his doubt ends and mine begins.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that the critical voice you've been living with isn't originally yours, it was handed to you by someone who may have meant well but left you carrying his doubt as if it were truth. And there's something quietly sad in the way you said that, like you're only just beginning to grieve the confidence that got quietly taken from you before you even had a chance to build it. I'm curious — now that you can see that voice has a source outside of you, does it feel even a little bit less like *your* truth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... yeah, a little, I guess. Like, hearing you say it out loud makes it feel more real that it came from him and not just from... me being actually bad at things. But then there's this other part of me that immediately pushes back and says, "well, what if he was right, and that's why it stuck so hard?"
therapist: That pushback your mind offers — "what if he was right?" — is actually one of the most common ways these old beliefs protect themselves, because if you can keep the doubt alive, you never have to risk finding out something different. But I want to sit with something you said: you noticed it felt *more real* that this came from him, even just for a moment — and that moment matters. What would it take for you to treat that small shift as evidence worth keeping, rather than letting the pushback immediately overwrite it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and yeah, that moment did feel different somehow, like it landed in a way that other things haven't. But here's the thing — I don't know how to hold onto something that fragile when the doubt comes rushing back in, which it always does, really fast. It's like trying to cup water in your hands, and by the time I'm even aware I'm doing it, it's already gone.
therapist: The image you just used — cupping water in your hands — is so honest and so precise, and it tells me you're not lacking awareness, you're lacking a container strong enough to hold these moments against the force of that old doubt. What we're doing here, actually, is starting to build that container — not by stopping the doubt from rushing in, but by practicing returning to that moment of recognition again and again until it becomes more familiar than the fear. So let's treat today as one of those repetitions — what's one small thing you could remind yourself of tonight, when the doubt comes back, that points to where that voice actually came from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea of a container, I really do, but I'm already kind of dreading tonight because that's usually when everything gets loudest in my head. I guess if I had to pick something to remind myself of, it would be that the voice telling me I'm not enough sounds exactly like my dad's voice, not my own. But I'm honestly not sure that knowing where it came from actually makes it quieter — it almost makes me feel worse, like I'm still carrying something that was never mine to carry in the first place.
therapist: What you just said — that knowing where it came from makes you feel *worse*, like you're grieving something that was never yours — is actually a really important and healthy part of this process, even though it hurts right now. That grief is real, and it makes sense that naming the burden can make its weight feel more visible before it starts to feel lighter. Tonight, when the voice gets loud, see if you can try saying to yourself: "This isn't mine to carry" — not to make it disappear, but just to remind yourself that you're allowed to set it down.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that phrase could help. But honestly, when the voice gets loud at night, it feels so much like me, like it's coming from inside me, that I'm not sure I'd even be able to separate it enough to say "this isn't mine." It's like trying to tell yourself a dream isn't real while you're still inside it.
therapist: The dream analogy is really beautiful and accurate — and what strikes me is that you're describing it in this very quiet, almost resigned way, like you've already accepted that tonight will be hard before it's even arrived. That acceptance isn't weakness, but I wonder if underneath the words there's also something that feels a little exhausted by all of this — not just the voice, but the effort of trying to fight it. What would it feel like to not fight it tonight, but just notice it, the way you might notice a dream starting to fade when you wake up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think you're right that I'm exhausted... it's like I've been bracing for the anxiety to hit every single night for so long that the bracing itself has become its own kind of weight. But I'm not sure I understand what "just noticing" would actually look like in practice, because every time I try to just observe the voice, it feels like I'm giving it permission to get louder. What if not fighting it just means it wins?
therapist: The fear that noticing means losing is actually one of the most common things that keeps people locked in the exhausting cycle of bracing — but here's the reframe: the voice only "wins" if it goes unexamined, and noticing is actually the opposite of surrender, it's the first act of not being fully controlled by it. In practice, "just noticing" might look as simple as saying to yourself, "there's that voice again," the way you'd note rain on a window — not inviting it in, not slamming the glass shut, just acknowledging it's there without making it mean something about you. I'm curious — does the bracing you described, that constant preparation for the anxiety, ever actually make the nights feel safer, or has it just become automatic?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when you put it that way — "there's that voice again" — it sounds almost too simple, like it couldn't possibly be enough to do anything. But I guess if I'm being honest, the bracing doesn't actually make the nights feel safer, it just feels like the only thing I have control over, even if it's exhausting. It's become so automatic that I'm not even sure I'd know what to do with myself if I stopped doing it.
therapist: What you just admitted is really significant — that the bracing isn't actually protecting you, it's just the illusion of control in a moment where everything else feels uncertain, and letting go of it feels almost scarier than the anxiety itself. That makes complete sense, because we tend to hold tightest to the things that feel like *something* rather than risk having nothing, even when that something is exhausting us. I'm wondering — if the bracing didn't exist, what do you imagine you might actually need in those quiet nighttime moments instead?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
